The brine that fills the pump vault carries dissolved exchanger salts, and the salts eat
light. Four metres is the whole of it. At four metres a hand-lamp shows the diver her own
glove; at five it shows nothing, and the beam does not fade into a dimness that a patient
eye can read - it stops. There is no silhouette, no glow, no reflected edge, no shape
against a lighter water. Past four metres the vault is not dark in the way a room with the
lights off is dark. It is not there.

So nothing in the vault is ever established by looking at it. A diver knows the cradle
because her hand is on the cradle. She knows the ring is unbroken because she has run a
thumb around it, or because she has pinged it and read the return in her teeth, and the
return tells her the shape of a thing and nothing about its colour or its condition. And a
ping is not free: it is a sound in a small flooded room, and it tells anyone else in the
water exactly where she is and that she wanted to know something.

The vault is eleven metres from the throat to the core cradle. Two people at opposite ends
of it are, to each other, a voice on a wire and nothing else.
